chunks: Musa ibn al-Qasim narrated from Safwan and Ibn Abi Umayr, from Ibn Muskan, from al-Halabi, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:
I said to him: A man performed tawaf around the House (Kaaba) and shortened one lap (shawt) in the Hijr (area adjacent to the Kaaba). He said: 'He must repeat that lap.'
Abd al-Jabbar narrated from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Ishaq ibn Ammar, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man performed tawaf around the House, then went out to al-Safa and performed tawaf between al-Safa and al-Marwah. While he was performing tawaf, he remembered that he had left some of his tawaf around the House. He said: 'He returns to the House, completes his tawaf, then returns to al-Safa and al-Marwah and completes what remains.'

And whoever doubts his tawaf and does not know whether he performed six laps or seven: if his tawaf was for the obligatory duty, he must repeat it from the beginning; and if his tawaf was for the voluntary (nafl) prayer, he should build upon the lesser number (six) and complete seven. And if he went out (to al-Safa) and then doubted, there is no penalty upon him.

key_terms.الصَّفَا وَالْمَرْوَة: Al-Safa and Al-Marwah: The two hills between which pilgrims walk during Sa'i
key_terms.الْحِجْر: Al-Hijr: The semi-circular wall area adjacent to the Kaaba
key_terms.شَوْط: Shawt: A single lap or circuit of the tawaf
key_terms.طَوَاف: Tawaf: Ritual circumambulation of the Kaaba

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling if a pilgrim doubts the number of tawaf laps or leaves the Kaaba before completing it?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* details the jurisprudential nuances of *tawaf* errors, emphasizing the principle of returning to the point of interruption to maintain ritual continuity. It distinguishes between obligatory (*fard*) and voluntary (*nafl*) circumambulations, prescribing strict repetition for the former and leniency for the latter, reflecting the Shia emphasis on precision in worship. The ruling on doubt (*shakk*) highlights the pragmatic application of the 'presumption of continuity' (*istishab*) in ritual law.
